The published pass prices are admission prices. Arrange transport and guide services separately and check the quoted inclusions.
Must I visit at sunrise?
No sunrise visit is assumed in this route. Choose a departure time that matches the current visitor schedule and your group’s preferences.

stories.title: Dadaocheng for beginners: a slower Taipei afternoon
stories.dek: Start with Dihua Street, leave space for tea and use the visitor centre to shape an outing that fits your time.
body: Choose Dadaocheng when you want a Taipei afternoon built around a neighbourhood rather than a ticketed landmark. Dihua Street provides the starting point, with a visitor centre and market area that help orient a first visit. Our suggested route keeps the focus narrow so you can spend time browsing instead of travelling between unrelated districts.

The tourism administration presents Dihua Street as a way to understand the city’s past. Read that background alongside the shops you see today, without expecting every business to function as a museum. The aim here is to give you a practical order for exploring, not to claim an inspection of individual shops.

p: Taipei’s official visitor-centre page places it on Dihua Street opposite Yongle Market. That makes it a useful orientation stop for this outing. Check its current schedule if you want help or a particular activity; you can still plan an outdoor visit without relying on an interior being open.

Ask about the area you want to explore rather than collecting a large list of attractions. Our suggestion is to choose one street segment, one browsing stop and one refreshment break. If an activity needs a reservation, treat that as a separate booking rather than a guaranteed walk-in option.

sections.h: Browse Dihua Street with a purpose
p: Tea, everyday trading and heritage streetscape give Dihua Street its appeal. Decide whether you are looking for a gift, interested in shopfronts or simply hoping to sit down for a drink. That choice will make it easier to spend time in the shops that interest you.

When buying tea or packaged goods, ask about the size, price and what is included before ordering. A tasting may have its own terms. Check the rules for any goods you intend to take home; this guide does not make customs or import guarantees.

sections.h: Use Yongle Market as an orientation point
p: The market and visitor centre provide a useful pair of reference points rather than a promise of a particular stall being open. Save the meeting location if members of your group want to browse independently. Allow extra time when shopping requires comparing fabrics or other products.

If the weather or your energy changes, shorten the browsing section and keep the seated stop. You do not need to add a second shopping district to make this an enjoyable afternoon. Choose what fits the time you have and use current directions for the return trip.

sections.h: Plan the journey and the spending separately
p: Taipei’s tourism site provides MRT journey and fare information. Check the route from your own starting point, then compare the walk from the station with a bus connection if you prefer. Do not assume the nearest station is also the most convenient exit for your group.

Budget for getting there and back, one drink or meal, and a separate shopping allowance. The outdoor neighbourhood visit does not include a bundled ticket, tasting or workshop. For a shorter version, explore the area around the visitor centre and return after a break rather than trying to cover the whole street.

quickPlan: First-time visitors who want a flexible, neighbourhood-focused plan.
Allow 2–3 hours for browsing and one seated stop; add more time if shopping becomes the main activity.
Separate MRT or bus fares from refreshments and shopping. Set a spending limit before browsing tea and gifts.

No tasting is included in this route. Check availability, prices and booking conditions with the shop you choose.

stories.title: Hong Kong’s harbour: plan one crossing well
stories.dek: Link Central and Tsim Sha Tsui with the Star Ferry, with time on each shore and a flexible return journey.
body: A harbour outing can be a satisfying introduction to Hong Kong without becoming a day-long transport challenge. Our suggestion is to concentrate on Central, one Star Ferry crossing and Tsim Sha Tsui, then decide whether you want to return by ferry or continue elsewhere. Keep other island trips and viewpoints for a separate plan.

The Hong Kong Tourism Board describes Star Ferry connections between Central or Wan Chai and Tsim Sha Tsui. This guide chooses Central for a simple starting point, not because every ferry uses the same pier or departure pattern. Read the destination signs before joining a queue.

sections.h: Find the correct pier before the queue
p: The tourism board identifies the Central Star Ferry Pier at Central Pier 7. Save that name when planning the journey from your hotel rather than navigating only to the broad waterfront area. Include the walk from your arrival station or bus stop in the time you set aside.

Ask staff if you are unsure which queue is for your destination and deck. A pier name and a sailing time are not interchangeable. This guide deliberately avoids quoting an unverified next departure or promising that the wait will be short.

sections.h: Choose the deck and check the fare
p: The tourism board notes that ferry fares vary between decks and between weekdays and weekends. Check the displayed fare for the sailing you intend to take. Treat transport cards and payment options as a practical choice, with any card purchase or deposit kept separate from the ride fare.

A brief crossing is still a transport journey: allow time for boarding and follow crew instructions. Our suggestion is to enjoy the view without building the entire outing around a particular seat or photograph. If a sailing changes, adjust the shore-side time instead of rushing to preserve a rigid schedule.

sections.h: Give each shore a different purpose
p: Use Central for the start and Tsim Sha Tsui for a break and a look back across the harbour. Choose a seated meal or a shorter refreshment stop before deciding how far to continue on foot. You can have a good outing without adding another paid attraction.

Our planning allowance is 2–3 hours for the combined shore time and crossing, not the duration of the ferry trip. If you have only an hour, choose one waterfront area and leave the crossing for later. If you have longer, make a deliberate second plan rather than automatically adding an outlying island.

sections.h: Keep a return option and a separate budget
p: The tourism board also explains MTR, buses and other city transport. Before starting, save a route back from the far shore so you have an alternative to retracing your ferry journey. Service conditions and accessibility can differ; consult operator information for the particular trip you need.

Make a small budget with four lines: travel to Central, ferry fare, refreshments and travel from the end point. No skyline show, attraction entry or cruise is included. That distinction helps you compare the simple harbour outing with more expensive experiences without assuming they provide the same service.

quickPlan: First-time visitors who want a flexible, neighbourhood-focused plan.
Allow 2–3 hours for the two shores and one crossing; queues and breaks are additional variables.
Check the ferry’s current deck and day-specific fare; add food and the journey to and from the piers separately.

No. This outing uses an ordinary Star Ferry crossing; a sightseeing cruise is a separate product with its own route and price.
Do I have to return by ferry?
No. Check an MTR or bus route from your final location before starting, then choose the return that fits your plan.

stories.title: Paris by the Seine: two islands at a slower pace
stories.dek: An outdoor-first walk around Île de la Cité and Île Saint-Louis, with optional interiors kept outside the basic plan.
body: You do not need to fit every Paris landmark into your first outing. The two central Seine islands offer a compact focus, with river views and time to stop between crossings. Our suggested plan is an outdoor walk, leaving cathedral or monument interiors as choices that you book and budget separately.

Paris je t’aime connects Île de la Cité and Île Saint-Louis in its island walk and identifies Pont Saint-Louis as the link between them. We use that geographical connection for an adaptable outing. Some operational statements in the tourism article are dated, so its historic descriptions are not treated here as confirmation of today’s entry arrangements.

sections.h: Start with a meeting point on Île de la Cité
p: Choose a visible meeting point and save it before leaving your accommodation. The island includes the Notre-Dame area, but the route does not require cathedral entry. Look at the exterior and the surrounding public space without treating a visitor queue as part of the basic walking allowance.

If an interior is your priority, check that venue’s own current booking information first, then build the walk around the actual appointment. Do not infer access from older tourism descriptions or from another attraction’s admission rules.

sections.h: Cross Pont Saint-Louis and slow down
p: The tourism board describes Pont Saint-Louis as the bridge connecting the two islands for pedestrians and cyclists. Use it as the middle of the outing, then explore a manageable section of Île Saint-Louis rather than hurrying to another distant landmark.

Our suggestion is to decide at the crossing whether you want a longer wander or a seated break. Give other people room to pass when stopping for a photograph. A bridge view is a useful pause, not a reason to block the route while coordinating a large group.

sections.h: Separate the river walk from paid visits
p: The island walk includes references to the Conciergerie and other heritage sites. Consider them optional interiors, each with its own visitor conditions. If you want one, select it in advance and confirm the entry rules directly rather than assuming a general city pass covers your date and activity.

For an outdoor-focused afternoon, keep your main costs to transport and what you choose to eat or drink. This guide does not claim every surrounding venue is free, and a river cruise is not part of the walking route. Read inclusions carefully when comparing a guided tour with independent exploring.

sections.h: A shorter version and the route home
p: For a shorter outing, stay around Île de la Cité and make the bridge your turning point. For the full 2–3-hour version, include time on the second island and a café pause. These are planning allowances, not measured walking times; crowds and your pace will change the experience.

Save a public-transport return from your chosen end point before you set off. Airport transfers are a different journey and should have their own ticket and route check. If this is your departure day, leave a substantial separate transfer window rather than fitting the walk immediately before check-in.

stories.title: Istanbul in two outings: old-city culture and a ferry day
stories.dek: Give Sultanahmet its own time, then pair Karaköy with Kadıköy on a separate harbour-focused outing.
body: Istanbul rewards a plan that leaves room between its different neighbourhoods. Our suggestion is to divide a first visit into two outings: a historic-area half-day around Sultanahmet, followed on another day by Karaköy and a ferry to Kadıköy. This gives you a choice of atmosphere without implying that the whole city fits into one checklist.

GoTürkiye presents Sultanahmet alongside contemporary cultural areas such as Karaköy and Kadıköy. Şehir Hatları lists a Kadıköy–Karaköy–Eminönü ferry route. Those official references provide context and a transport connection, while the suggested order and time allowances below are our editorial planning choices.

p: Choose one interior you most want to visit, or keep the outing outside around the historic area. GoTürkiye lists major landmarks here, but their admission categories, booking arrangements and visiting rules need separate checks. A square, a place of worship and a ticketed monument are different types of visit.

If your chosen site has a timed booking or restricted visiting periods, build around that first. Leave space for a meal or seated break rather than moving directly from one queue to another. This guide does not quote a single combined admission price for the district.

sections.h: Make Karaköy the beginning of another outing
p: GoTürkiye includes Karaköy among Istanbul’s walkable cultural neighbourhoods. Use it as a starting point for a shorter stroll and a refreshment stop before the ferry. Decide whether you want street-level exploring or a particular gallery visit, because a booked interior changes the available time.

Save the actual departure pier and check the destination shown on the sailing. Do not treat all waterfront stops as interchangeable. Our recommendation is to finish any shopping before joining the queue, so you can keep the crossing and the far-shore plan straightforward.

The municipal ferry operator lists the Kadıköy–Karaköy–Eminönü service. Consult its current timetable for your direction and day rather than relying on a general statement that boats are frequent. Choose a return option before departure and leave room to adapt if service conditions change.

Once across, give Kadıköy time as a neighbourhood rather than a quick photograph before the return. Pick a compact area for food or browsing and keep the walk within your available time. A regular ferry journey is not the same product as a dedicated sightseeing cruise.

sections.h: Compare two half-days with one long day
p: If you have one afternoon, choose either the historic-area outing or the ferry-focused plan. Our two-outing version is intended to reduce the number of unrelated stops competing for your time. It is not a promise that either half-day covers every attraction in its neighbourhood.

Use separate budget lines for city transport, ferry fare, refreshments and optional entry. Ask a tour provider what is included if you decide to book a guide. Keep the airport journey outside this allowance, especially because Istanbul’s two main airports require different transfer planning.

quickPlan: First-time visitors who want a flexible, neighbourhood-focused plan.

Separate monument admission from ferry fares and food; check current visitor categories and displayed prices.

You can shorten both, but this guide suggests separate half-days so bookings, transfers and breaks do not compete for the same time.

No. The listed municipal ferry connection is a transport service. Compare any sightseeing cruise separately by route, duration and price.

stories.title: Hanoi beyond the Old Quarter: choose your cultural afternoon
stories.dek: Compare the Temple of Literature with the Vietnamese Women’s Museum, then give one place time instead of chasing both.
body: A second Hanoi outing can add context to the streets you explored on your first day. The useful question is not how many monuments you can collect, but which kind of story you want to spend time with. Our suggestion is to choose either the Temple of Literature or the Vietnamese Women’s Museum as the main visit, with a break afterwards.

Vietnam Tourism links the temple to the city’s educational history and describes the museum through artefacts, costumes, crafts and personal accounts. Those are different subjects, not interchangeable attractions. Use the comparison below to decide which fits your interests; this guide does not claim a personal inspection of either collection.

sections.h: Choose the temple for architecture and education
p: The Temple of Literature, also called Văn Miếu, was established in 1070 and became associated with the university Quốc Tử Giám in 1076. Its courtyards and scholarly records make it a useful choice if you want an architectural setting as well as historical context.

Our suggestion is to allow 60–90 minutes inside, then pause before deciding whether to go elsewhere. Read the interpretation you find rather than treating the courtyards simply as a sequence of photographs. This is an editorial allowance, not a measured visit duration.

sections.h: Choose the museum for people and material culture
p: The Vietnamese Women’s Museum offers another way into the country’s history and society through objects and personal accounts. If you prefer reading exhibition interpretation to walking through an architectural complex, make this your principal stop.

Pick two subjects that interest you and give them attention rather than trying to absorb every label. Leave time to compare objects, photographs and the stories accompanying them. If your group reads at different speeds, agree on a meeting point instead of hurrying each other through the rooms.

sections.h: Keep the two locations separate in your plan
p: Do not assume this comparison is a short walking circuit. Save the address of the venue you choose and plan the journey from your accommodation. If you later add the other venue, include the transfer as a separate part of the outing.

The linked tourism overview contains admission and schedule information that may be older than current venue arrangements. We use it for cultural background and do not carry those prices into a guaranteed present-day budget. Check the venue’s current notice before making a special journey.

sections.h: Turn the visit into a useful afternoon
p: Reserve a little time afterwards to talk over one object, courtyard or historical detail you remember. A café break gives the visit an ending without automatically turning it into another sightseeing stop. For a shorter outing, keep only the principal venue and the journey home.

For costs, separate admission, local transport and refreshments. Ask about visitor categories and any booked activity rather than assuming a general entry price includes a guided tour. If you are short of time, comparing the subjects in advance is more useful than buying two tickets and rushing both.

quickPlan: Temple for architecture and education; museum for social history and material culture.
Our suggestion: 2–3 hours for one principal visit, transfers and a break.
Check current admission directly; add transport and refreshments separately.
faq: Which should I visit first?
Choose by subject rather than ranking: temple architecture and educational history, or museum collections about women’s roles and lives.
Are both included in one ticket?
No combined admission is assumed. Check each venue’s current visitor information before paying.

stories.title: Siem Reap without another temple: a craft-focused afternoon
stories.dek: See making as well as finished objects at Artisans Angkor, and keep the town craft centre distinct from the silk-farm outing.
body: After a temple day, another long circuit is not the only way to spend time in Siem Reap. A craft-focused afternoon can shift the attention from monumental buildings to how things are made. Our starting point is Artisans Angkor’s town craft centre, with the silk farm treated as a separate option.

This is an independently written planning guide using the operator’s visitor information. It is not a paid placement, an inspection of working conditions or an endorsement of every product in the boutique. We have no booking commission from the reference link.

sections.h: Choose the town craft centre first
p: Artisans Angkor places its Siem Reap craft centre on Chantiers-Ecoles Stung Thmey Street and advertises guided visits. Save the location and check the current arrangement for your intended date, especially if you want a particular tour language or activity.

Our suggestion is to allow 60–90 minutes for the visit and browsing, then decide whether to extend the outing. Ask how much of the making process you can observe that day. A workshop visit does not automatically mean visitors can use tools or join a hands-on session.

sections.h: Observe a process before choosing a purchase
p: Give yourself a simple question to follow: what material is being worked, what stage are you seeing, and what comes afterwards? That makes the visit useful even if you buy nothing. Ask staff before photographing artisans or handling unfinished objects.

If a finished piece interests you, compare its size, material and price with what you can actually take home. Request packing information for fragile objects and a receipt for any purchase. Browsing is a different activity from commissioning a made-to-order item.

sections.h: Keep the silk farm as a separate decision
p: The operator also lists an Angkor Silk Farm visit showing stages from silkworms through weaving. It is not the same location as the town craft centre. Before adding it, ask about its current visitor arrangements and the transport required between the two.

Our recommendation is to choose the town visit for a compact afternoon and the silk farm when the textile process is your main interest. Do not let the word “craft” make two different locations appear to be one walk-in attraction. No shuttle, transfer or combined ticket is assumed here.

sections.h: Make space for a town break afterwards
p: Leave the end of the outing open for a meal or a seated drink rather than booking another activity immediately after the workshop. If your temple morning ran long, shorten the shopping part instead of treating it as an appointment you must complete.

Plan transport, any activity charge, refreshments and shopping as separate budget lines. Ask the operator to confirm what the visit includes; this guide intentionally does not promise free entry or an included workshop where the current page does not establish those terms.

quickPlan: Visitors interested in materials, making and a shorter town outing.
Our allowance: 60–90 minutes at the town craft centre, plus your journey and a break.
Confirm visit or activity charges; keep shopping and any silk-farm transfer separate.
faq: Can I make my own souvenir during the visit?
A hands-on session is not assumed. Ask the operator about available activities, eligibility, booking and fees.
Is the silk farm part of the town visit?
It is listed as a separate location. Confirm transport and visiting arrangements before combining the two.

stories.title: Beitou’s Hot Spring Museum: culture before a soak
stories.dek: Plan a free museum visit, understand the Monday closure and keep any bathing experience as a separate booking.
body: Beitou’s name may suggest a bathing outing, but the Hot Spring Museum serves a different purpose. Its official visitor information says it is a cultural display space and does not provide hot-spring services. That distinction matters if you are comparing a museum afternoon with a paid bath or hotel package.

Our suggestion is to use the museum as the anchor of a modest cultural visit, with travel and a refreshment break around it. A separate soak is optional. We do not recommend an unverified bath operator or make health claims about hot-spring water.

sections.h: Check the day before setting off
p: The museum’s official page lists free admission, Tuesday–Sunday opening from 10am to 6pm and last entry at 5:45pm; Monday is closed. These details were consulted on 9 October 2026. Check for special closures before travelling.

Our planning allowance is 45–75 minutes inside. Do not mistake last admission for a comfortable arrival time: arriving just before it leaves little room to read displays. If the museum is the reason for the trip, arrange the journey so the visit is not compressed into closing time.

Visitors are normally asked to change into the museum’s provided slippers. Food and drink are restricted to designated areas, and staff may manage admission when capacity is reached. Follow the instructions at the entrance rather than assuming a free museum has unrestricted access.

If the footwear arrangement or waiting procedure does not suit your needs, contact staff before the visit. Leave food for the break afterwards so you can focus on the displays. Keep photography and movement considerate of other readers and the historic building.

sections.h: Plan the journey without bundling the whole district
p: Use Taipei’s official MRT information to check a journey to the Beitou area from your starting point, then save the museum address at 2 Zhongshan Road. Check the final walking directions and your preferred return connection separately.

This guide does not turn every nearby attraction into a compulsory stop. If you want a longer outing, choose one additional activity based on its own current access information. A shorter version is simply the museum, a break and the journey back.

sections.h: Keep a bathing plan in its own budget
p: If a soak is your priority, compare a bath operator’s actual services, appointment rules and price before choosing. Museum admission does not include bathing, towels, changing facilities or a hotel room. Those are separate services even when their names refer to the same district.

For a museum-only outing, the main budget lines are transport and refreshments, because the listed museum admission is free. Add a paid bathing service only after deciding how long it takes and how you will get home. The goal is a plan that fits your interests, not a bundle inferred from a place name.

quickPlan: Readers interested in Beitou’s cultural history, with bathing optional.
Our suggestion: 45–75 minutes inside, plus travel and a seated break.
Museum admission is listed as free; Monday closed. No bathing service is included.

No. Its official visitor page explicitly says it does not provide hot-spring services.

The published regular schedule closes on Mondays. Check the museum’s current notices before planning an exception.

stories.title: Hong Kong by tram: make your first ding-ding ride easy
stories.dek: Choose a direction, pay on exit and use one ordinary ride as part of a neighbourhood outing.
body: A tram ride gives a different perspective from the harbour crossing in our first Hong Kong guide. This outing stays on Hong Kong Island and uses an ordinary public tram, rather than a sightseeing tour with commentary. The useful first decisions are where you want to board and which direction your destination lies.

Hong Kong Tramways lists six main routes, with termini extending between Kennedy Town and Shau Kei Wan. Not every tram runs the whole length. Use the destination sign and the operator’s current route information instead of boarding whichever vehicle arrives first.

p: Our suggestion is to choose one neighbourhood for a break and use the ride to get there. Central, Wan Chai and Causeway Bay appear among the operator’s along-the-tracks areas. A named district alone is not a stop instruction: save the stop you actually want.

Check whether you need an eastbound or westbound service and whether the tram’s displayed destination takes you far enough. If you are uncertain, confirm before boarding rather than discovering at a terminus that you need another journey.

sections.h: Understand the fare and exit payment
p: The operator’s fare page lists the ordinary adult fare as HK$3.30, consulted on 9 October 2026. It says fares are paid when leaving through the front exit; cash users need the exact amount because no change is given. It also lists electronic payment methods.

Two separate ordinary adult rides would therefore total HK$6.60 at that published fare, before any other transport. This is arithmetic for a simple return plan, not a day pass or a tour price. Confirm the current fare notice before travelling.

sections.h: Give the ride a flexible place in the afternoon
p: Allow a broad slot rather than promising an exact journey time on busy city streets. Our suggestion is a ride followed by 30–60 minutes in the neighbourhood you choose. If you have an appointment, compare a more direct transport option and keep the tram outing for another time.

A seat on the upper deck is optional, not a guaranteed inclusion. Choose a position you can use comfortably and follow boarding instructions. If you need particular accessibility arrangements, consult the operator for that service rather than assuming the whole fleet offers the same access.

sections.h: Separate public transport from a tour product
p: Hong Kong Tramways also advertises TramOramic sightseeing and charter services. Their booking terms and prices are separate from the ordinary fare. Decide whether you want everyday transport or a narrated experience before comparing what you will pay.

Keep the neighbourhood break modest on a first ride: one place to look around and somewhere to sit is enough. Save a return route before stepping off. That could be another tram or a different public-transport connection; returning by the same vehicle is not part of an ordinary single-ride fare.

quickPlan: An ordinary tram ride and one Hong Kong Island neighbourhood break.
Published adult fare HK$3.30 per ordinary ride; two rides HK$6.60, excluding other costs.
Pay at the front exit; carry exact cash if using coins because no change is given.
faq: Does an ordinary ride include a sightseeing guide?
No commentary or guided tour is assumed. Compare TramOramic or charter products separately.
Does every tram run to Shau Kei Wan?
No. The operator lists several routes; check the displayed destination and current route information.

stories.title: A Paris history afternoon at Musée Carnavalet
stories.dek: Use the free permanent collection as your main visit, with temporary exhibitions and group bookings handled separately.
body: A museum afternoon can give the city a different kind of context from a river walk. Musée Carnavalet focuses on the history of Paris, and its official visitor information makes a useful distinction: individuals can visit the permanent collections free without booking, while temporary exhibitions have separate conditions.

Our suggestion is to choose the permanent collection for a focused first visit, then add a break afterwards. This is a research-based planning guide, not a review claiming we inspected every room or attended the current exhibition.

sections.h: Choose the visit type before making a reservation
p: For an individual permanent-collection visit, the museum lists free access without a booking. Temporary exhibitions are charged separately and the museum strongly advises booking for a specific date and time. An activity with a museum guide is also a distinct service.

Group visits have their own reservation arrangements, even when the collection itself is free. If you are organising a group, use the relevant booking information instead of applying the individual rules. A free collection does not mean every museum experience costs nothing.

sections.h: Arrive with enough time to read
p: The published regular schedule is Tuesday–Sunday, 10am–6pm. Last admission to the permanent collection is 5:15pm and rooms close at 5:45pm; holidays and special dates may have exceptions. These details were consulted on 9 October 2026.

Our suggestion is to allow 90 minutes to two hours inside rather than arriving just before the last-entry deadline. Pick a few periods or objects to follow, and leave room to read their context. Trying to finish every room is not required for a useful first visit.

sections.h: Find the visitor entrance and travel light
p: The official visitor entrance is at 23 rue Madame de Sévigné. The museum lists several public-transport options, including Saint-Paul on Metro Line 1. Check the journey from your actual starting point rather than assuming one station suits every traveller.

The museum restricts luggage and large bags. Do not plan the visit as a place to spend several hours with suitcases before an airport transfer. Read the current bag rules and choose a separate luggage arrangement if needed.

sections.h: Build a low-cost afternoon around one collection
p: For this particular plan, permanent-collection entry is free, while transport and refreshments remain your own costs. Choose a break after the museum rather than expecting every visitor service or nearby café to be part of the admission arrangement.

If you want the temporary exhibition too, compare its booking time with the amount of attention you have left. A shorter version is a focused permanent-collection visit only. On a day the museum is closed, use a different plan rather than relying on an older general list of free Paris museums.

quickPlan: Paris history through a focused permanent-collection visit.
Our suggestion: 90 minutes–2 hours inside, plus travel and a break.
Individual permanent collections: free without booking. Temporary exhibitions and group arrangements differ.

Can I bring a suitcase?

stories.title: Istanbul’s bazaars: choose what you want to browse
stories.dek: Compare the Grand Bazaar with the Spice Bazaar and keep shopping, food and the journey between them in separate parts of the plan.
body: A bazaar visit works better when you have a reason to browse. If you want textiles, decorative objects or a broad covered-market experience, compare the Grand Bazaar first. If food products and spices interest you more, start with the Spice Bazaar. Our suggestion is to choose one as the main visit rather than promise a complete shopping circuit.

GoTürkiye describes the commercial area between the two through Eminönü and its variety of specialist shops. That is useful context, not evidence that every shop has the same opening time, price or product quality. This guide makes no partnership or commission claim for an individual seller.

sections.h: Start with the kind of shopping you enjoy
p: The Grand Bazaar’s tourism profile highlights products such as carpets, teapots and lamps, while the Spice Bazaar profile centres on edible goods and spices. Use those broad differences to choose your starting point. Do not assume the shorter shopping list is the shorter visit if you intend to compare purchases carefully.

For a browsing-only outing, set a time limit and leave a little of it for finding your chosen exit. For a buying trip, focus on one product category so you can ask useful questions about size, material, quantity and total price.

sections.h: Agree what the displayed price refers to
p: Before paying, establish whether a quoted amount refers to one item, a set, a weight or a package. Ask about packaging and any additional charge. If you are only looking, say so clearly instead of treating a demonstration as a promise to buy.

For food products, read the label and ask what is included before choosing. For fragile or bulky objects, consider how you will transport them before deciding a lower price is a better purchase. This guide does not certify product origin, authenticity or export suitability.

sections.h: Treat the second bazaar as optional
p: If you want both, save a route between your actual entry and exit points and allow a break. The tourism board’s description of an area connecting markets should not be read as an exact walking-time guarantee. Street conditions, browsing and your own pace change the outing.

For a shorter plan, choose one bazaar and one meal or drink nearby. Do not add the ferry day from our other Istanbul guide automatically: shopping bags, departure queues and a second neighbourhood make it a different trip.

sections.h: Make the spending plan before you arrive
p: Separate transport, refreshments and purchases in your budget. A shopping allowance is a personal limit, not an estimated ticket price for the bazaar. No bargaining result or cheapest-shop claim is promised here.

If you buy a gift, request a receipt and keep a note of the shop’s contact details. Check relevant transport and destination rules for anything you plan to take home. Finish with enough time to locate your return connection rather than using the last moments of the outing on one more purchase.

quickPlan: Grand Bazaar for broad craft and decorative browsing; Spice Bazaar for food-product interests.
Our suggestion: 90 minutes–2 hours for one main bazaar, plus refreshments and transport.
Set a separate shopping limit; transport and refreshments are additional personal costs.
faq: Must I visit both bazaars?
No. Choose the market that suits your interests first; the second is optional, with its own journey and browsing time.
Does this guide recommend a particular seller?

stories.title: Tokyo solo travel: an easy first day in Asakusa
stories.dek: One neighbourhood, a temple approach and a riverside pause: a flexible first-day plan with room for lunch and finding your way home.
quickPlan: Asakusa Station → Kaminarimon and Nakamise → Senso-ji → an optional Sumida riverside pause.
Our suggested allowance: 3–4 hours, including lunch and breaks.
Separate rail travel, meals and shopping; add tickets only for an optional paid activity.
stories.researchNote: An editorial route for independent visitors, informed by an observed solo-travel search theme. It is not a guided tour, on-site review or safety rating. Local details checked against GO TOKYO on 9 October 2026.
body: For your first solo day in Tokyo, start with a neighbourhood you can leave easily when you have had enough. Asakusa gives the outing a clear shape: arrive at the station, follow the temple approach, choose somewhere for lunch, then decide whether to continue towards the river. You can enjoy the main walk without committing to an evening reservation or another cross-city journey.

The useful question is how much to put in this first day. Our answer is one main area and one optional extension. This suggested route suits travellers who want to practise using local transport and ordering a meal while keeping the day manageable. It also works as a shorter outing after a tiring arrival, provided you allow yourself to stop early.

sections.h: Save your arrival and return before leaving the hotel
p: GO TOKYO lists the Ginza, Toei Asakusa and Tobu Skytree lines at Asakusa Station. Choose the line that fits your accommodation and save the return journey separately. A shared station name does not tell you which platform or exit you will need; check the route and signs when you arrive.

Keep the name and address of your accommodation available offline. Put your phone charging cable and any required transport payment within reach before leaving. These small preparations let you use the first part of the morning for finding your bearings rather than searching for a booking email at a station entrance.

sections.h: Use the temple approach as the main outing
p: The tourism board places Kaminarimon, the Nakamise shopping street and Senso-ji together in its Asakusa guide. Use those landmarks to organise the walk. Browse at your own pace, leave room for other visitors and check any photography notices before stopping for a picture.

Set a shopping allowance before you start browsing. If you like something, check the total price and whether it fits your luggage rather than buying it just because the next shop looks busy. Keep your route flexible: a crowded shopping street is a reason to slow down or take a break, not a reason to squeeze another district into the day.

Choose lunch when you are ready to sit down, rather than relying on a sequence of snacks to carry the whole outing. Read the menu and prices before entering, ask whether a seat for one is available and check the ordering method. If the queue is longer than you want to wait, keep another option in the same area.

For a first meal, a clear menu and comfortable seat may matter more than a famous name. Keep dietary requirements written in a form the venue can understand and confirm them with staff. This route does not endorse an individual restaurant or promise that every business can meet every request.

sections.h: Make the river the optional finish
p: The official area guide also covers the Sumida waterfront. After lunch, decide whether a riverside pause still sounds enjoyable. Check the actual walk from where you are and leave the extension out if the weather, your energy or your return plans make a shorter day preferable.

A boat trip is a separate booking decision. Check the operator’s current departure point, destination and timetable before buying a ticket; a riverside walk does not require you to take a cruise. End the outing with enough energy to find your return platform, and save an evening activity for another day if you would prefer an early dinner.

faq: Is this a full-day Tokyo itinerary?
No. It is a suggested 3–4 hour Asakusa outing with lunch and an optional river pause. Travelling from your accommodation takes additional time.
Do I need to book a tour for this route?
The suggested walk is self-guided. Any cruise, performance or other paid experience needs its own access and booking check.

stories.title: A slow Taipei weekend: two days without a packed itinerary
stories.dek: Pair a Dadaocheng afternoon with a separate Beitou culture outing, using one main area per day and keeping meals and transport flexible.
quickPlan: Dadaocheng: trading streets, a browsing stop and a seated meal.
Beitou: plan around the museum’s opening day, with bathing optional and booked separately.
Our suggestion: one main district each day, with unscheduled time before and after.
stories.researchNote: A two-day editorial framework inspired by the slow-travel search theme, not evidence that Taipei is currently a rising Google Trends destination. Sources consulted 9 October 2026.
body: A slower Taipei weekend starts by choosing what to leave out. Give Dadaocheng one afternoon and Beitou a separate day instead of combining both with a long list of city landmarks. You still need to check transport and opening times, but you can leave space for a meal, a change in weather and the shop you actually want to browse.

This plan is for visitors who prefer fewer transfers and longer pauses. It does not require a particular hotel or a shopping budget. Keep your accommodation as the starting point for both days, and decide how much walking is comfortable before adding anything else. The two outings can be swapped if the museum’s opening day makes that more practical.

sections.h: Day one: choose a reason to browse Dadaocheng
p: Taipei’s tourism board describes Dihua as a district associated with tea, groceries, herbs and clothing, alongside historic shopfronts. Pick the part that interests you most. A tea-focused visit and a fabric-shopping visit will lead to different stops, even when they share the same street.

Before leaving, select one starting landmark and a place where you can pause for a meal. Do not turn every interesting shop into a required stop. If you are buying gifts, decide what you can carry and ask about the size and contents of each package. Browsing is already a worthwhile activity; you do not need to buy something to complete the afternoon.

sections.h: Leave a real gap around your meal
p: Use lunch or an afternoon drink as the flexible part of day one. If a business is busy, choose between waiting and moving on before ordering. Keep enough room in the schedule to sit down rather than treating the meal as another landmark to tick off.

Take a note of the shops you may want to revisit. Returning to one place tomorrow is an option, not a failure of the itinerary. If rain interrupts the afternoon, shorten the walk and keep the shopping list. This guide does not promise sheltered access between every stop or a fixed opening time for independent businesses.

sections.h: Day two: make Beitou a culture outing first
p: Plan the Beitou visit around the Hot Spring Museum. Its published visitor information gives Tuesday–Sunday opening from 10am to 6pm, with last admission at 5.45pm; admission is free. Recheck the museum’s own notice before travelling, especially around holidays or a temporary closure.

The museum visit and bathing are different activities. Start by deciding whether you want to learn about the area or spend time in a bathing facility. For a culture-only day, you can finish after the museum and a meal. If a soak matters to you, choose the facility separately and check its current price, booking method and visitor rules.

sections.h: Keep transport and the second activity separate
p: Check the metro journey from your own accommodation for each outing, including the return. A route between two attractions is less useful than a clear plan from your actual starting point. Save a station name and a meeting point if you are travelling with someone who may explore independently.

Before adding an evening market or another museum, ask what it would replace: a rest, a meal or an earlier return. Choose one optional extra at most. A slower weekend is successful when the time feels comfortable, not when the route has the greatest number of pins. Keep bookings limited to activities you would be disappointed to miss.

faq: Can I use this plan on Monday?
Dadaocheng can be considered separately, subject to individual business opening times. Do not schedule the museum for a regular Monday; its published schedule is Tuesday–Sunday.
Is a Beitou bath included?
No. The museum is a cultural visit. A bathing facility is a separate choice with its own charges and rules.

stories.title: Mexico City food outing: a market lunch or a guided tour?
stories.dek: Choose the format that fits your appetite, language needs and budget, then plan around one market instead of a race between famous dishes.
quickPlan: Consider Mercado San Juan–Arcos de Belén for a lunch-focused visit; save its exact map pin.
Compare a specific operator’s meeting point, inclusions, walking distance and dietary policy before booking.
Our suggested allowance: 2–3 hours for one market outing, plus your transport.
stories.researchNote: An independent planning guide prompted by Google’s April 2026 report on Mexico City food searches. That report is historical context, not a live October ranking. The cover shows Palacio de Bellas Artes, not the market. No tour operator is endorsed.
body: Choose the kind of food outing you want before choosing a list of dishes. If you are comfortable reading menus, asking prices and deciding where to stop, a single market lunch can give you a flexible afternoon. If explanation, a shared group or help with ordering matters more, compare a guided tour with clearly stated inclusions.

Both formats can work, but they solve different problems. A market visit gives you control over the pace and spending. A booked tour gives you a planned sequence and an agreed meeting point. Neither format guarantees the best meal in the city, and a search trend cannot tell you which operator or stall will suit your preferences.

sections.h: For lunch, save the correct San Juan market
p: The city’s tourism guide distinguishes Mercado San Juan–Arcos de Belén from San Juan–Pugibet. Its Arcos de Belén listing highlights fondas serving lunch and places the market by Eje Central and Metro Salto del Agua. Save the full market name and its map location rather than searching only for “San Juan”.

Use that listing as a starting point for a lunch outing, not a promise of today’s menu. When you arrive, look at the available meals and ask the total price before ordering. Decide whether you want a seated meal or a smaller tasting stop; trying to do both everywhere quickly makes the outing less enjoyable.

Start with one main meal and leave room for one additional stop if you still want it. Separate the amount you intend to spend on food from transport and take-home purchases. Keep your return journey available on your phone before you start browsing.

Ask what a menu price includes, whether a drink is separate and what payment method the business accepts. If ordering feels difficult, pause and find a clearer menu rather than agreeing to a price you do not understand. A few written food preferences can help the conversation, but the venue must confirm what it can provide.

sections.h: Guided: compare the actual booking, not the headline
p: For a guided outing, make a short comparison using the operator’s current page. Record the meeting point, language, group size if stated, duration, food inclusions and any separate costs. A tour described as a food walk may include several tastings, a full meal or neither unless the description says so.

Check how much walking and standing is involved and whether the route has planned breaks. Send dietary questions before paying, and read the cancellation and late-arrival terms. Do not assume a higher price guarantees more food or a smaller group. This guide has no affiliate booking link and does not rank an operator it has not assessed.

sections.h: Give the afternoon an easy finish
p: After the meal, decide whether to continue exploring or return to your accommodation. A second market needs another journey and another appetite; it should be optional rather than part of a compulsory food circuit. Keep any non-food stop flexible so a queue or longer lunch does not make you late for a reservation.

Write down what you enjoyed and the market’s full name if you want to recommend it later. Before sharing a stall recommendation, distinguish your own meal from a broad claim about the whole market. The most useful result of the outing is a meal and a format you enjoyed, not a claim that you found the city’s universal best.

faq: Do I need a food tour to eat at a market?
A tour is optional. A self-guided lunch suits visitors comfortable choosing a venue and arranging their own transport; a guided format can offer explanation and a planned sequence.
Are both San Juan market names interchangeable?
No. The city tourism listing distinguishes Arcos de Belén from Pugibet. Save the exact name and location for the place you intend to visit.

places.name: The Grand Palace and Wat Phra Kaew
places.hours: Ticket sales 8:30am–3:30pm; consult the official schedule for closing times
places.blurb: The royal compound founded in 1782 and the temple that houses the Emerald Buddha, Thailand's most revered image. Shoulders and knees must be covered. Go at opening time, before the tour groups and the heat.

places.name: Wat Pho
places.hours: Daily 8am–7:30pm, as listed on the official planning page
places.blurb: A temple complex known for its reclining Buddha and traditional massage school. Plan the temple visit and any massage separately.

places.name: Wat Arun
places.hours: TAT lists daily 8am–6pm; confirm with the temple
places.blurb: The Temple of Dawn, whose central spire is covered in pieces of coloured porcelain. Take the cross-river ferry from Tha Tien pier, beside Wat Pho. It looks its best from the opposite bank at sunset.

places.name: Wat Saket (the Golden Mount)
places.blurb: A gilded chedi on top of an artificial hill. More than 300 steps wind up past bells and gongs to a terrace with an open view over the old city.

places.name: Jim Thompson House Museum
places.blurb: Six traditional teak houses joined into one home by the American who revived the Thai silk trade and vanished in Malaysia in 1967. The main house is seen by guided tour only, offered in five languages. Address: 6 Soi Kasemsan 2, Rama 1 Road, a short walk from BTS National Stadium.

places.name: Bangkok Art and Culture Centre
places.blurb: A spiral of free contemporary art galleries opposite MBK Center, linked directly to BTS National Stadium. The lower floors hold small design shops and cafes.

places.name: Lumphini Park
places.blurb: Bangkok's central park, laid out in the 1920s. Joggers circle the lake at dawn and dusk, and large monitor lizards sun themselves on the banks. MRT Silom and Lumphini are at the corners.

places.name: Talat Noi
places.blurb: A riverside neighbourhood of Chinese shrines, car-part workshops and street art, between Chinatown and Charoen Krung. Landmarks include the So Heng Tai mansion and the Holy Rosary Church.

places.name: Pak Khlong Talat (flower market)
places.blurb: The city's wholesale flower market, near Memorial Bridge and MRT Sanam Chai. Marigold garlands, orchids and jasmine are sold by the armful around the clock.

places.name: Chatuchak Weekend Market
places.hours: Weekend general market; midweek plant and Friday wholesale sessions differ. Check the visitor website for your day.
places.blurb: A large market for clothes, ceramics, plants, antiques and food. Choose the general weekend market if you want the broadest browsing; plant and wholesale sessions are different outings. Save your entrance and return station.

places.name: Or Tor Kor Market
places.blurb: A clean, covered fresh market across the road from Chatuchak, known for top-grade fruit and a row of ready-to-eat curry stalls. MRT Kamphaeng Phet opens straight into it.

places.name: Jodd Fairs Ratchada
places.blurb: The Ratchada location is distinct from the former Rama 9 market.

places.name: Train Night Market Ratchada
places.blurb: The Ratchada train market is behind Esplanade, separate from Jodd Fairs.

places.name: Rot Fai Market Srinakarin
places.blurb: A separate train-market location in the Srinakarin area.

places.name: Ong Ang Canal walking street
places.blurb: A canal-side walking area near Chinatown.

places.name: Asiatique The Riverfront
places.blurb: A riverside retail and dining complex with additional paid attractions.

places.name: Thip Samai
places.blurb: The most famous pad thai in the city, cooked over charcoal since the 1960s. The premium version comes wrapped in a thin omelette. Expect a queue. MRT Sam Yot.

places.name: Raan Jay Fai
places.price: Confirm the current menu; seafood specialities can be a splurge
places.blurb: A well-known street-side kitchen associated with crab omelettes and wok-cooked seafood. Check the current menu and queue arrangements before visiting.

places.name: Nai Mong Hoi Thod
places.blurb: A small shophouse that does one thing: oyster omelette, fried crisp or soft. MRT Wat Mangkon.

places.name: Guay Jub Ouan Pochana
places.blurb: Rolled rice noodles in a clear pork broth that is heavy with white pepper, served on Yaowarat Road.

places.name: Boat Noodle Alley
places.blurb: A canal-side row of shops selling boat noodles in bowls that hold three mouthfuls. Stack the empties and count them at the end. BTS Victory Monument.

places.name: Go-Ang Pratunam Chicken Rice
places.blurb: Hainanese chicken rice served by staff in pink shirts on Phetchaburi Road. BTS Chit Lom.

places.name: Prachak Pet Yang
places.blurb: Roast duck over rice from a shop that has traded since 1909. BTS Saphan Taksin.

places.name: Jok Prince
places.blurb: Smoky rice porridge with pork balls and a century egg, eaten at breakfast.

places.name: Mae Varee
places.blurb: A fruit shop at the mouth of Sukhumvit Soi 55 that is known for mango sticky rice to take away.

places.name: King Power Mahanakhon SkyWalk
places.price: Ticketed. Prices vary by time of day
places.blurb: The city's highest observation deck: a glass floor at 310 metres and an open rooftop at 314 metres, with a bar at the top. Next to BTS Chong Nonsi.

places.name: Sky Bar at Lebua
places.blurb: An open-air bar on the 63rd floor of State Tower, familiar from the 2011 film The Hangover Part II. A smart dress code applies.

places.name: Vertigo and Moon Bar
places.blurb: A rooftop grill and bar on the 61st floor of the Banyan Tree hotel, with no walls and a view over Lumphini Park.

places.name: Octave Rooftop Lounge
places.blurb: Three levels on floors 45 to 49 of the Bangkok Marriott Hotel Sukhumvit, with a 360-degree view from the top. A short walk from BTS Thong Lo.

places.name: Mandarin Oriental, Bangkok
places.blurb: The city's oldest grand hotel, opened as The Oriental in 1876. The original Authors' Wing still serves afternoon tea.

places.name: The Peninsula Bangkok
places.blurb: A riverside hotel on the Thonburi bank. Compare the room category, boat services and current dining arrangements directly with the hotel.

places.name: The Siam
places.blurb: A riverside hotel in Dusit with an art and antiques focus. Compare current room categories, inclusions and transfers with the hotel.

places.name: Capella Bangkok
places.blurb: A Chao Phraya riverside hotel. Check the actual room category and included services rather than assuming every booking has the same view or benefits.

places.name: Wat Phra That Doi Suthep
places.area: Doi Suthep, 15 km from the old city
places.blurb: The mountain temple that watches over the city, founded in 1383. A staircase of 306 steps, flanked by naga serpents, leads to a golden chedi and a wide view. Red songthaews run up from the city.

places.name: Wat Chedi Luang
places.blurb: A huge brick chedi begun in 1391 and partly brought down by an earthquake in 1545. It once housed the Emerald Buddha that now sits in Bangkok.

places.name: Wat Phra Singh
places.blurb: Founded in 1345 at the west end of Ratchadamnoen Road. Its small Lai Kham chapel holds the revered Phra Buddha Sihing image.

places.name: Tha Phae Gate and the old city moat
places.blurb: The east gate of the square, moated old town and the city's meeting point. The whole old city is about a mile across and walkable.

places.name: Sunday Walking Street
places.blurb: About 1.1 km of stalls from Tha Phae Gate to Wat Phra Singh, with food courts set up in temple yards. At 6pm the national anthem plays and the whole street stands still. Most stalls take cash only.

places.name: Saturday Walking Street (Wualai)
places.area: Wualai Road, south of Chiang Mai Gate
places.blurb: A smaller, more local market of about 700 metres in the city's old silver-making quarter.

places.name: Warorot Market (Kad Luang)
places.area: Chang Moi, near the Ping River
places.hours: Indoor market 4am to 6pm · flower market 24 hours
places.blurb: The city's biggest daily market. Come for northern pork sausage sold by weight, dried fruit, and the flower stalls along the river.

places.name: Chiang Mai Gate Market
places.hours: Indoor 4am to 4pm · outdoor stalls 4pm to midnight
places.blurb: A working produce market by day that turns into one of the best-value places to eat in the evening.

places.name: Chiang Mai Night Bazaar
places.blurb: The big tourist market, spread along Chang Klan Road and through several covered arcades.

places.name: Kad Chin Haw (Friday morning market)
places.blurb: A small market run by the city's Yunnanese Muslim and Tai Yai communities, with food and produce that is rare elsewhere in Thailand.

places.name: Khao Soi Lam Duan Fa Ham
places.blurb: A khao soi shop that has traded for more than 70 years. The chicken curry noodle is the order. Address: 352/22 Charoen Rat Road.

places.name: Khao Soi Islam
places.area: Charoen Prathet Road, Night Bazaar area
places.blurb: A halal restaurant known for beef khao soi, near the Friday morning market.

places.name: Khao Kha Moo Chang Phueak
places.blurb: Braised pork leg over rice, served by a cook known across the city for her cowboy hat. It often sells out early.

places.name: The Big Buddha
places.blurb: A 45-metre seated Buddha faced in white marble, visible from much of the south of the island. The site closed after a landslide in August 2024 and reopened on 3 March 2026. Cover shoulders and knees. Sarongs are lent at the entrance.

places.name: Phuket Old Town
places.blurb: A few streets of pastel Sino-Portuguese shophouses built on tin-mining money. Thalang Road, Dibuk Road and little Soi Romanee are the prettiest.

places.name: Wat Chalong
places.blurb: The island's largest and most visited Buddhist temple, with a tall chedi that you can climb for a view.

places.name: Promthep Cape
places.blurb: The headland at the island's southern end and its most popular sunset spot. Come 45 minutes early for a place on the wall.

places.name: Lard Yai (Sunday Walking Street)
places.blurb: Southern Thai snacks, grilled skewers and craft stalls under the shophouse arcades. Arrive near 4pm for photographs and shorter queues. It gets crowded from 6pm.

places.name: Kata Beach
places.blurb: Kata Yai and Kata Noi are south-west coast beach options. Check current flags, patrol advice and conditions before deciding whether to enter the water.

places.name: Nai Harn Beach
places.blurb: A compact bay between green headlands, popular with residents. A freshwater lagoon sits just behind the sand.

places.name: Freedom Beach
places.blurb: A beach south of Patong with more involved access than a roadside beach. Confirm the permitted route, any charges and your return transport before setting out.

places.name: Mai Khao Beach
places.blurb: A northern Phuket beach listed by the provincial tourism office. Check permitted access and current local notices; do not approach restricted airport areas for photographs.

places.name: Patong Beach
places.blurb: The busiest beach and the island's nightlife centre. Bangla Road, just behind it, closes to traffic every evening.

places.name: Old Town breakfast shops
places.blurb: Phuket's cooking mixes Hokkien, Malay and southern Thai influences. In the old town, mornings mean dim sum from steamer baskets, yellow Hokkien noodles and strong kopi poured through a cloth filter.

places.name: Shwedagon Pagoda
places.blurb: A 99-metre gilded stupa and the most sacred Buddhist site in Myanmar. Four covered stairways climb the hill. Shoes and socks come off at the bottom, and shoulders and knees must be covered. Come an hour before sunset and stay as the lights come on.

places.name: Sule Pagoda
places.blurb: An octagonal golden stupa, about 46 metres tall, standing in the middle of a roundabout at the centre of the downtown grid.

places.name: Chaukhtatgyi Pagoda
places.blurb: A reclining Buddha about 65 metres long, housed in an open-sided iron shed. Look at the soles of the feet, which are covered in 108 sacred symbols.

places.name: Kandawgyi Lake
places.blurb: A park and boardwalk around a lake east of Shwedagon. The Karaweik, a concrete replica of a royal barge, sits on the eastern shore.

places.name: Yangon Circular Railway
places.blurb: A working commuter railway around Yangon. Historical descriptions of the loop are not a current timetable. Confirm the operating section, departure, carriage facilities and return before boarding.
places.hours: Confirm the actual operating section and return service at the station

places.name: Bogyoke Aung San Market
places.blurb: A covered market of more than 2,000 shops, known as Scott Market until 1948. Shop here for longyi, lacquerware, jade and tailoring.

places.name: 19th Street
places.blurb: A downtown street historically associated with barbecue restaurants. This listing is cultural background; confirm current businesses and local conditions before making plans.

places.name: 999 Shan Noodle Shop
places.blurb: A small shop behind City Hall known for Shan noodles, served sticky or in soup. Address: 130B 34th Street.

places.name: Lucky Seven
places.blurb: A traditional tea shop known for mohinga, the fish and rice-noodle soup that is Myanmar's national breakfast. Address: 130 49th Street.

places.name: The Strand
places.blurb: A colonial hotel opened in 1901 at 92 Strand Road, facing the river. Its cafe is known for afternoon tea.

places.name: Gardens by the Bay
places.blurb: A waterfront park opened in 2012. The outdoor gardens and the Supertree Grove are free to enter, and the grove puts on a light and sound show after dark. The two cooled conservatories are ticketed.

places.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
places.price: Free. The National Orchid Garden is ticketed
places.blurb: Founded in 1859 and listed by UNESCO in 2015, the country's first World Heritage Site.

places.name: National Gallery Singapore
places.blurb: The former Supreme Court and City Hall, joined into one museum of Southeast Asian art in 2015.

places.name: Maxwell Food Centre
places.blurb: One of the best-known hawker centres, opposite the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple. The longest queue is usually for Hainanese chicken rice.

places.name: Lau Pa Sat
places.blurb: A hawker centre under a Victorian cast-iron roof in the financial district. In the evening the street beside it closes to traffic and fills with satay stalls.

places.name: Petronas Twin Towers
places.blurb: At 452 metres, these were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004. Timed tickets cover the skybridge on levels 41 and 42 and an upper observation deck.

places.name: Batu Caves
places.blurb: A Hindu shrine inside a limestone cave, reached by 272 painted steps beside a 42.7-metre golden statue of Lord Murugan. KTM Komuter trains run from KL Sentral.

places.name: Jalan Alor
places.blurb: The city's best-known food street. After dark, tables fill the road and grills turn out satay, chicken wings and seafood.

places.name: Ben Thanh Market
places.blurb: The city's landmark covered market, built in 1914, with a clock tower over the south gate. Food stalls sit in the middle. Bargain for everything else.

places.name: Saigon Central Post Office
places.blurb: A working post office in a vaulted hall built between 1886 and 1891, opposite Notre-Dame Cathedral.

places.name: War Remnants Museum
places.blurb: A sobering museum of the Vietnam War, told through photographs, documents and military hardware in the courtyard.

places.name: Senso-ji
places.blurb: Tokyo's oldest temple, said to date to 645. Enter under the giant lantern of the Kaminarimon gate and walk up Nakamise, a street of snack and souvenir stalls.

places.name: Meiji Jingu
places.blurb: A Shinto shrine dedicated in 1920, set inside a planted forest of about 100,000 donated trees beside Harajuku station.

places.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
places.blurb: The wholesale fish auction moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the outer market's lanes of seafood, knife and tea shops are still here. Go in the morning. Many shops close in the early afternoon.
places.hours: Check the official calendar and individual shop hours

places.name: Shibuya Sky
places.blurb: An open-air deck about 229 metres up on the roof of Shibuya Scramble Square, opened in 2019. Sunset slots sell out, so book ahead.

places.name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
places.blurb: The main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty, first built in 1395. Visitors wearing hanbok enter free, and the guard-changing ceremony takes place at the main gate.

places.name: Gwangjang Market
places.blurb: A covered market that dates from 1905. The food alley is known for mung-bean pancakes fried to order and small seaweed rice rolls.

places.name: Euljiro
places.blurb: A district of print shops and hardware stores by day. In the evening, plastic tables fill the alleys for fried chicken and draught beer, and unmarked bars open upstairs.

places.name: The British Museum
places.blurb: Founded in 1753, with the Rosetta Stone and the Great Court's glass roof. Free to enter, with late opening on Fridays.

places.name: Tate Modern
places.blurb: Modern and contemporary art in a former power station on the Thames, opened in 2000. The collection displays are free.

places.name: Borough Market
places.blurb: London's best-known food market, on a site where traders have sold food for around a thousand years. It sits under the railway arches by London Bridge.

places.name: Miradouro da Senhora do Monte
places.blurb: A Graça viewpoint overlooking Lisbon and the Tagus. Save the exact approach; hillside streets and steps affect how you reach it.

places.name: Tram 28
places.area: Martim Moniz to Campo de Ourique
places.blurb: A vintage yellow tram that grinds through Graça, Alfama and Estrela. Ride early or late to get a seat, and watch your pockets.

places.name: Pastéis de Belém
places.blurb: The bakery that has made its custard tarts to the same recipe since 1837. The queue for takeaway is long, so walk in and find a table instead.

places.name: LX Factory
places.blurb: A former textile complex under the 25 de Abril Bridge, now shops, restaurants, studios and a large bookshop.

places.name: The High Line
places.blurb: A park 1.45 miles long, planted on a disused elevated freight railway. The first section opened in 2009.

places.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
places.blurb: Founded in 1870 and set on the edge of Central Park. One of the largest art museums in the world, so pick two or three departments and leave the rest.

places.name: Central Park
places.blurb: 843 acres in the middle of Manhattan. Enter at 72nd Street for Bethesda Terrace and the lake.

places.name: Joe's Pizza
places.blurb: A slice shop open since 1975 and a fair place to learn what a New York slice is: thin, crisp at the base and folded to eat.

places.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
places.blurb: The country's great museum of its pre-Hispanic civilisations, opened in 1964. The Aztec Sun Stone is in the Mexica hall.

places.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
places.blurb: A white marble opera house and museum with murals by Diego Rivera and other Mexican masters on its upper floors.

places.name: Mercado de Coyoacán
places.blurb: A neighbourhood market known for its tostada counters, a few blocks from the Frida Kahlo museum.

places.name: Café Tortoni
places.blurb: The city's most famous cafe, founded in 1858, with marble tables, stained glass and waiters in waistcoats.

places.name: El Ateneo Grand Splendid
places.blurb: A bookshop inside a theatre that opened in 1919. The stage is now a cafe and the boxes are reading nooks.

places.name: Feria de San Telmo
places.blurb: An antiques and street market that runs along Calle Defensa every Sunday, with tango dancers in Plaza Dorrego.

places.name: Bondi to Coogee coastal walk
places.blurb: Six kilometres of clifftop path linking beaches and ocean pools, including Bronte Baths and Wylie's Baths, which opened in 1907.

places.name: Bondi Icebergs Pool
places.blurb: A 50-metre ocean pool at the south end of Bondi, home to a winter swimming club founded in 1929. Casual swimmers pay a small entry fee.

places.name: Sydney Opera House
places.blurb: Jørn Utzon's building opened in 1973 and joined the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2007. Walk around it for free, or book a tour or a performance.

places.name: Royal Botanic Garden
places.blurb: Established in 1816 on the harbour's edge, with the classic view back to the Opera House and the bridge.

places.name: Table Mountain
places.blurb: The 1,086-metre flat-topped mountain behind the city. A cableway with rotating cars has run since 1929 and closes in high wind. The most direct walk up is the Platteklip Gorge path.

places.name: Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden
places.blurb: Founded in 1913 on the mountain's eastern slope and devoted to South African plants. A curved treetop walkway crosses the arboretum.

places.name: Bo-Kaap
places.blurb: Steep cobbled streets of brightly painted houses, the historic home of the city's Cape Malay community. People live here, so ask before photographing doorways.

places.name: Hong Kong Tramways ordinary services
places.blurb: Ordinary public tram journeys with several destinations. Check the displayed route and current fare before boarding.

places.name: Musée Carnavalet – Histoire de Paris
places.blurb: Free permanent collections for individual visits; charged temporary exhibitions and group reservations have separate terms.

places.name: Grand Bazaar

places.name: Spice Bazaar

events.title: The Weeknd
events.blurb: Three stadium nights. Allow extra time for the journey out.

events.title: Jason Mraz
events.blurb: One night at the Bangkok International Trade and Exhibition Centre, beside BTS Bang Na.

events.title: Bangkok Art Biennale
events.blurb: Four months of contemporary art across the city, including installations inside working temples.

events.title: BABYMONSTER
events.blurb: Two nights for the K-pop group.

events.title: My Chemical Romance
events.where: Impact Challenger Hall, Muang Thong Thani
events.blurb: One night only.

events.title: Loy Krathong
events.where: Chao Phraya riverside: Wat Arun, Wat Yannawa, Asiatique
events.blurb: On the full-moon night, people float small candle-lit baskets on rivers, canals and park lakes. Published dates differ by a day, so check the local programme.

events.title: BTS
events.blurb: Shows on 3, 5 and 6 December.

events.title: Wonderfruit
events.where: The Fields at Siam Country Club, near Pattaya
events.blurb: A music, art and food festival about two hours from Bangkok.

events.title: Saturday Walking Street
events.blurb: The smaller weekly market, in the old silver quarter.

events.title: Sunday Walking Street
events.blurb: The big weekly market, from Tha Phae Gate to Wat Phra Singh.

events.title: Yi Peng and Loy Krathong
events.where: Tha Phae Gate, Three Kings Monument, Wat Phan Tao, Ping River
events.blurb: The northern lantern festival. Free events fill the old city. Sky lanterns may only be released at licensed, ticketed venues outside town.

events.title: Phuket Vegetarian Festival
events.blurb: Nine days honouring the Nine Emperor Gods: dawn street processions, firecrackers and meat-free food stalls under yellow flags. The opening pole-raising is on the evening of 9 October.

events.title: Lard Yai Sunday market
events.blurb: The weekly walking street under the shophouse arcades.

events.title: EDC Thailand
events.blurb: A three-day electronic music festival.

events.title: Thadingyut, the Festival of Lights
events.blurb: The end of Buddhist Lent. Homes, streets and pagodas are lit with candles and lanterns, and people pay respects to parents and teachers. The full-moon day is 26 October.

events.title: Tazaungdaing full moon
events.blurb: The second festival of lights, marking the end of the rainy season. Robe-weaving contests are traditionally held overnight at Shwedagon.

events.title: National Day
events.blurb: Offices and many shops close.

events.title: Deepavali
events.blurb: Deepavali is listed as Sunday 8 November by the Ministry of Manpower. Monday 9 November is a public holiday for those whose rest day falls on Sunday. Check the separate Little India programme for light-up and bazaar dates.

events.title: Shichi-Go-San
events.blurb: Families bring children aged three, five and seven to shrines in formal kimono. Weekends either side are just as busy.

events.title: Bonfire Night
events.blurb: Fireworks displays mark Guy Fawkes Night. Most big displays are ticketed and fall on the nearest weekend.

events.title: The Lord Mayor's Show
events.where: Starts at Mansion House, City of London
events.blurb: A procession more than three miles long through the City. Free to watch. Roads are closed, so come by Tube or train.

events.title: São Martinho
events.blurb: St Martin's Day is marked with roast chestnuts from street braziers and the first taste of the year's new wine.

events.title: Village Halloween Parade
events.blurb: Giant puppets, bands and thousands of costumed marchers. Anyone in costume can join.

events.title: TCS New York City Marathon
events.blurb: Held on the first Sunday of November through all five boroughs. Watch from First Avenue or from Brooklyn's Fourth Avenue.

events.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
events.where: Central Park West to Herald Square
events.blurb: Giant balloons and marching bands on Thanksgiving morning. Arrive before dawn for a kerbside spot.

events.title: Día de Muertos
events.blurb: Families build altars of marigolds, candles and food for relatives who have died. Public altars fill the Zócalo.

events.title: Sculpture by the Sea
events.blurb: About 100 sculptures along two kilometres of clifftop path. Free. Go on a weekday morning.
